nodes.id: Accommodation, Food Services, Arts and Entertainment
nodes.label: Industry
nodes.overview: The Accommodation, Food Services, Arts and Entertainment industry (ransomware.live sector tag "Hospitality and Tourism") is a high-frequency, high-visibility ransomware target: 771 victims have been tracked on ransomware.live's leak-site monitoring platform since roughly 2018, spanning hotels, casinos, restaurants, theme parks, cruise lines, museums, theaters, and travel/tour operators across 65+ countries (with the US, GB, FR, ES, CA, AU, DE and IT most represented). The sector is attacked by a broad spread of ransomware groups -- LockBit (in its 2/3/5 variants), Qilin, Akira, Play, Medusa, IncRansom, RansomHub, DragonForce and Clop are the most prolific -- and has produced some of the highest-profile ransomware incidents in history (MGM Resorts, Caesars Entertainment) due to the combination of large, valuable guest/loyalty databases, PCI-regulated payment systems, IT/OT-blended physical operations (casino floors, digital key/lock systems, POS), heavy third-party/franchise dependency, and a business model highly sensitive to even brief guest-facing downtime -- all of which make organizations in this sector both frequent targets and comparatively willing payers.
nodes.distinct: 771 tracked victims across 65+ countries spanning hotels, casinos, restaurants, theme parks, cruise lines and museums. Distinctively franchised and multi-site, with inconsistent security maturity across properties and heavy seasonal revenue concentration. Casino and gaming operations add regulator-supervised systems and cage/loyalty data. Guest-facing outages are immediately public and directly convert to booking loss and brand damage.
nodes.extortion_leverage: Guest-facing service disruption timed to peak periods, combined with exposure of guest PII, payment card data and loyalty records.
nodes.downtime_tolerance: Low to moderate. Days in the ordinary course, but effectively hours during peak season or a major event, when a single weekend outage can absorb a quarter's margin.

nodes.id: Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Food Production
nodes.label: Industry
nodes.overview: The Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Food Production sector is a designated critical-infrastructure sector (Food & Agriculture / FA) that has become one of the fastest-growing ransomware targets. It spans a "farm-to-fork" chain of primary producers (crop farms, livestock/poultry, dairy, aquaculture/fisheries, forestry/timber), cooperatives and grain elevators, agri-input suppliers (seed, fertilizer, agrochemicals), food and beverage processors/manufacturers, cold-storage and logistics providers, and grocery/food distributors. The sector's defining risk characteristic is an extraordinarily low tolerance for downtime: perishable inputs and finished goods spoil, livestock require continuous feeding/climate control, and processing is time-and-temperature critical, so an IT outage rapidly cascades into physical, food-safety and food-security consequences. This combination — thin IT/OT security maturity, seasonal/just-in-time operations, heavy automation (SCADA in plants, precision-ag telematics, automated milking/feeding), and consolidation that concentrates single points of failure (a handful of meatpackers, one dominant grocery distributor) — makes victims unusually likely to pay ra
nodes.distinct: A designated critical-infrastructure sector and one of the fastest-growing targets, spanning farm-to-fork from primary producers through cooperatives, processors, cold-storage and distribution. Defining characteristic is perishability: unlike any other sector, the inventory itself degrades during an outage, so downtime destroys assets rather than merely deferring revenue. Heavy concentration in a few large processors and cooperatives controlling large throughput shares, paired with generally low security maturity among producers, creates food-security consequence at national scale.
nodes.extortion_leverage: Spoilage-driven urgency and disruption of processing and cold chain, amplified by food-security and public-health visibility.
nodes.downtime_tolerance: Extremely low during harvest, processing and cold-chain operation — hours before irreversible product loss; higher in off-season and administrative functions.

nodes.id: Construction
nodes.label: Industry
nodes.overview: The Construction sector (general contractors, engineering/design firms, infrastructure operators, homebuilders, specialty trades, and building-materials suppliers) is one of the most heavily and consistently targeted industries by ransomware groups. Ransomware.live's full victim dataset shows 1,362 distinct Construction-sector victims posted to ransomware leak sites from 2019 through mid-July 2026, with volume climbing sharply from 2021 onward and 2025 alone accounting for 513 posted victims - more than any prior full year (2026 already shows 267 through mid-July). The sector combines several features attackers find attractive: large numbers of small/mid-size subcontractors with weak security maturity sitting inside supply chains for very large general contractors and government owners; time-sensitive, contractually penalized project schedules that increase pressure to pay quickly; large transient, multi-employer workforces with sprawling credential/access footprints; and high-value intellectual property (design/BIM data, bids, proprietary engineering methods) alongside sensitive employee PII (payroll, SSNs) in HR/finance systems. Victims range from small regional contractors to th
nodes.distinct: 1,362 distinct victims posted 2019 through mid-July 2026, with 2025 alone accounting for 513 — more than any prior full year, and 267 already recorded through mid-July 2026. Distinguished by project-based rather than continuous operations, low IT maturity relative to revenue, and a highly fragmented subcontractor web that widens the trust boundary. Bid and tender data is uniquely sensitive: its exposure creates competitive rather than regulatory harm. Government-owner project work pulls public-sector data and clearance obligations into scope.
nodes.extortion_leverage: Exposure of confidential bid, contract and design data plus project schedule delay and associated liquidated damages; encryption leverage is comparatively weaker.
nodes.downtime_tolerance: Moderate to high. Days to weeks. Physical site work continues during an IT outage, though payroll, procurement and design-file access degrade progressively.

nodes.id: Educational Services
nodes.label: Industry
nodes.overview: The ransomware.live Education sector dataset returned 1,296 named victims spanning 2016 through 20 July 2026. Volume by year shows the sector's escalation and persistence: 2016 (2), 2017 (1), 2018 (2), 2019 (4), 2020 (15), 2021 (74), 2022 (157), 2023 (307), 2024 (248), 2025 (328), and 158 already recorded in the first ~7 months of 2026. 2023 and 2025 are the peak full years; the 2024 dip did not hold, and 2026 is tracking broadly in line with recent years. Attribution is highly fragmented, with 135 distinct groups named. The top claimants across the full period are lockbit3 (114), qilin (73), incransom (72), vicesociety (63), rhysida (57), pysa (50), medusa (45), clop (44), ransomhub (43), and safepay (39); the top ten groups account for only 46.3% of postings, confirming a long tail of smaller and short-lived brands. Composition has shifted materially: restricting to 2025-2026, the leaders become qilin (65), incransom (47), safepay (29), interlock (25), thegentlemen (24), lockbit5 (19), fog (19), nova (18), shinyhunters (14), and rhysida (13) - i.e. LockBit-era dominance and the education-specialist Vice Society and PYSA brands have been displaced by Qilin, INC Ransom, Interlock a
nodes.distinct: 1,295 tracked victim records, rising from 15 in 2020 to 307 in 2023 and 328 in 2025, with 157 already in the first seven months of 2026 — a sustained upward trajectory. Heavily US-concentrated (519 of 946 country-attributed records) and dominated by LockBit3 (114), Qilin (73), INC Ransom (72), Vice Society (63) and Rhysida (57); the prominence of Vice Society and Rhysida reflects deliberate specialization in schools and universities as soft, data-rich, under-defended targets. Distinctive combination of open-by-design networks, BYOD and research-collaboration culture, minors' data raising notification sensitivity, and constrained appropriated budgets that limit both prevention spend and ranso
nodes.extortion_leverage: Exposure of student records including minors' data, staff PII and research IP, plus disruption timed to enrollment, examination and term-start pressure points.
nodes.downtime_tolerance: Moderate to high in absolute terms — days to weeks absorbed by academic calendars — but sharply lower at term start, enrollment and examination periods. Weak budget capacity for both ransom and rapid restoration means outages run longer than tolerance alone would predict.

nodes.id: Energy and Utilities
nodes.label: Industry
nodes.overview: The Energy and Utilities sector (ransomware.live tag "Energy," ~826 indexed victim records at time of research) spans oil & gas exploration/production, pipelines and midstream transport, refining, oilfield services, electric power generation/transmission/distribution, gas distribution, and water/wastewater utilities. It is a top-tier ransomware target because it blends two high-leverage traits: (1) it is critical national infrastructure where downtime has cascading physical, economic, and public-safety consequences, giving attackers extraordinary extortion leverage; and (2) it runs a large, aging, and often flat-networked mix of IT and operational technology (OT/ICS/SCADA). Even when malware only hits corporate IT, operators frequently shut down OT preemptively out of caution (as Colonial Pipeline and Conpet did), so IT-only intrusions still cause operational and physical-world disruption (fuel shortages, offline payment at fuel retail, halted shipment planning). Financially the sector is among the most expensive to recover: Sophos put mean recovery cost for energy/oil-gas/utilities at ~$3.12M (2024), IBM put average energy-sector breach cost at $4.83M, and the sector reports the h
nodes.distinct: Roughly 826 indexed victims across oil and gas, pipelines, refining, power generation and transmission, and water/wastewater. Blends critical-national-infrastructure status — where downtime carries cascading physical, economic and public-safety consequence — with large, aged, geographically dispersed OT estates. Uniquely, the precautionary IT/OT shutdown is itself the loss event: operators halt physical operations defensively when IT is compromised, as Colonial Pipeline showed, so business interruption occurs even where OT is never touched. Heaviest regulatory overlay including CIRCIA and sector-specific mandates.
nodes.extortion_leverage: Threat to physical operational continuity and public-safety consequence, giving attackers extraordinary leverage disproportionate to the data actually held.
nodes.downtime_tolerance: Extremely low. Minutes to hours for grid, pipeline and water operations, where interruption is a public-safety and regulatory event, not merely a commercial one.

nodes.id: Finance and Insurance
nodes.label: Industry
nodes.overview: Finance and insurance is one of the most consistently targeted industries in the ransomware threat landscape, combining three features attackers prize: high-value, tightly regulated data (PII, account/payment details, claims and underwriting data); low tolerance for downtime given real-time payment, trading, and claims obligations; and deep interdependency through vendors, fintech partners, and market infrastructure that lets a single compromise cascade well beyond one victim. Recent ransomware.live data (100 most-recent sector-tagged victims, spanning roughly April-July 2026) shows the sector being hit across the full spectrum of institution types - community banks and credit unions, insurers and brokers, wealth/asset managers, fintech and payments firms, and even a central bank - by a wide range of groups (Qilin, Everest, DragonForce, Akira, Everest, LockBit successors, Lapsus$, and newer entrants like Unsafe and Krybit), with double-extortion (encrypt-and-exfiltrate) now the dominant pattern. Notable historical and recent incidents illustrate two especially distinctive hazards for this industry versus others: (1) systemic/market-contagion risk, where ransomware against a market-
nodes.distinct: Combines the highest-value regulated data with real-time payment, trading and claims obligations and dense interconnection through fintech partners and market infrastructure that permits contagion beyond the direct victim. Generally the most mature sector in controls, capital and recovery capability, which lowers payment likelihood while raising regulatory and systemic-risk scrutiny under GLBA and, for EU-touching entities, DORA.
nodes.extortion_leverage: Exposure of customer PII/PFI, account and counterparty data, plus regulatory and market-confidence consequence. Availability leverage is real for payments and trading but blunted by mature redundancy.
nodes.downtime_tolerance: Very low for transaction processing and settlement (minutes to hours); moderate for back-office and underwriting functions.

nodes.id: Healthcare and Social Assistance
nodes.label: Industry
nodes.overview: Healthcare and Social Assistance is one of the most heavily targeted sectors in the ransomware ecosystem, driven by a combination of low tolerance for downtime (patient safety), high-value PHI, fragmented and legacy IT/OT environments, and a long tail of small, under-resourced providers (clinics, home health agencies, billing firms) alongside a handful of giant, deeply interconnected health systems and claims processors. Ransomware.live's "Healthcare" sector tag currently lists 2,443 posted victims spanning 2015-2026 (dataset pulled 2026-07-19/20), with the pace of incidents accelerating sharply since 2020 (34 in 2020 vs. 627 in 2025 and 387 already in the first ~6.5 months of 2026). The threat-actor landscape is fragmented across 206 distinct named groups in the dataset, with Qilin (178), LockBit3 (143), Inc Ransom (128), BianLian (92), RansomHub (81), Clop (72), ALPHV/BlackCat (68), Everest (63) and Medusa (63) the most prolific against this sector. Geographically the US dominates (1,092 recorded victims), followed by the UK (58), Australia (58), Canada (57), India (56), Germany (55), France (47) and Brazil (45), reflecting both the concentration of large private health systems i
nodes.distinct: 2,443 posted victims with sharply accelerating pace. The only sector where both extortion levers are simultaneously severe: PHI carries the most punitive and mechanically triggered regulatory regime (HIPAA breach notification, OCR investigation, near-automatic class-action follow-on), while downtime is a patient-safety event producing ambulance diversion and delayed treatment. Fragmented estates, unpatchable connected medical devices, and a long tail of small under-resourced providers sit alongside a few giant claims processors whose compromise cascades industry-wide.
nodes.extortion_leverage: Dual: patient-safety-driven urgency to restore clinical operations, plus PHI publication carrying regulatory penalty and litigation exposure.
nodes.downtime_tolerance: Lowest of any sector. Hours for clinical and emergency systems, where outage translates directly into patient harm rather than financial loss alone.

nodes.id: Information Technology
nodes.label: Industry
nodes.overview: The Information Technology sector (software vendors, IT-services/MSPs, SaaS/cloud hosts, distributors, semiconductor/EDA and telecom-adjacent firms) is one of the two most-targeted industries in ransomware, consistently ranking behind only manufacturing. Its defining risk feature is systemic/aggregation exposure: IT companies sit upstream of thousands of downstream customers, so a single intrusion into an MSP platform (Kaseya), a managed file-transfer product (MOVEit/Progress), a SaaS provider (CDK Global), or a distributor (Ingram Micro) cascades into mass downstream outages and data loss far larger than the direct victim. Beyond encryption-based extortion, the sector is disproportionately exposed to data-theft/leak extortion and intellectual-property theft (source code, chip designs, product blueprints). Common initial-access paths are the sector's own internet-facing edge (VPNs, RMM tools, MFT appliances), leaked/infostealer credentials, and exploitation of vulnerabilities in products the companies themselves ship. Regulatory exposure is intensifying (SEC cyber-disclosure rules, GDPR, breach-notification statutes, and large class-action liability). Sector-level economics per Sop
nodes.distinct: One of the two most-targeted industries, behind only manufacturing. Its defining feature is systemic aggregation exposure: software vendors, MSPs, SaaS hosts and distributors sit upstream of thousands of customers, so a single intrusion cascades into mass downstream outage and data loss — Kaseya, MOVEit, CDK Global and Ingram Micro each proved this at scale. For a cyber portfolio this is the sector most capable of generating a single correlated accumulation event across an entire book, and privileged remote-management access makes IT firms both victim and weapon.
nodes.extortion_leverage: Downstream customer impact and reputational destruction of the platform, plus source code, IP and customer data theft. Contractual liability to thousands of customers often dwarfs the insured's own restoration cost.
nodes.downtime_tolerance: Very low. Minutes to hours for SaaS and hosting under contractual SLAs, with customer attrition and contractual penalties beginning almost immediately.

nodes.id: Manufacturing
nodes.label: Industry
nodes.overview: Manufacturing has been the single most-targeted sector by ransomware operators for five consecutive years through 2025, driven by a combination of high operational-downtime sensitivity (which pressures victims toward paying quickly), widespread reliance on legacy OT/ICS equipment with long refresh cycles, deep tiered supply-chain interdependency that multiplies contingent business-interruption exposure, and valuable intellectual property/trade-secret data. The ransomware.live "Manufacturing" sector tag alone contains 4,434 recorded victim postings, with year-over-year posting volume roughly quadrupling from 2021 (295) to 2025 (1,204), and the sector accounting for an estimated one in four ransomware attacks globally by 2025 per industry trackers. Attack economics are shifting: per Sophos's 2025 manufacturing-specific report, successful encryption rates have fallen sharply (74% to 40% YoY) as defenses improve, but attackers are compensating by shifting toward pure data theft and extortion, and average ransom demands against manufacturers have risen even as median demands/payments across all sectors trend down. High-profile incidents — from Norsk Hydro's ~$70M LockerGoga attack (2019
nodes.distinct: The most-targeted sector for five consecutive years through 2025, with 4,434 leak-site postings. Combines legacy OT/ICS estates on decade-plus refresh cycles with deep tiered supply-chain interdependency and valuable trade-secret data. A weak IT/OT boundary means an IT-side encryption event routinely halts physical production, and a single Tier-2 supplier outage idles multiple OEMs, producing contingent business interruption invisible on the direct victim's own policy.
nodes.extortion_leverage: Production downtime. Ransom is priced against per-hour output loss and contractual delivery penalties, secondarily against theft of designs, process IP and trade secrets.
nodes.downtime_tolerance: Very low. Hours to a few days; continuous-process and just-in-time operations tolerate least, and idle-line cost accrues immediately regardless of data outcome.

nodes.id: Professional, Scientific, Technical Services, Real Estate and Wholesale Trade
nodes.label: Industry
nodes.overview: This composite industry group spans consultancies, IT/managed services, law and accounting firms, engineering firms, staffing and BPO providers, travel management companies, commercial real estate services, and wholesale/logistics distributors. Ransomware.live's 'Business Services' sector tag is one of the most heavily populated on the platform, logging dozens of new claimed victims per week in mid-2026, with RaaS/extortion groups Qilin, DragonForce, INC Ransom, TheGentlemen, Akira, RansomHouse, Deadlock, and data-extortion crews like ShinyHunters posting new victims almost daily. The sector's risk profile is distinctive because these firms sit at a structural chokepoint: (1) they hold sensitive, often privileged or regulated client/third-party data (legal, financial, M&A, PII) that amplifies extortion leverage; (2) many are themselves suppliers/vendors (MSPs, SAP integrators, BPOs, staffing firms, travel managers) whose compromise cascades into downstream client organizations, making them attractive 'one-to-many' targets; and (3) wholesale trade/logistics operations depend on time-sensitive order, warehouse, and freight systems where even short outages create cascading supply-chai
nodes.distinct: One of the most heavily populated leak-site categories, logging dozens of new claimed victims weekly in mid-2026. Spans consultancies, MSPs, law and accounting firms, engineering, staffing/BPO, commercial real estate and wholesale distribution. The defining feature is custodianship of other organizations' confidential material: privileged legal files, audit workpapers, M&A data and client PII. A single firm's breach becomes many clients' breach, and MSPs within this group double as an access path into downstream victims.
nodes.extortion_leverage: Confidentiality of privileged and client-owned data, with professional-liability, contractual and regulatory consequence flowing to clients rather than only the insured.
nodes.downtime_tolerance: Moderate to high. Days to weeks for most advisory work; wholesale/logistics sub-segments are materially tighter due to order and fulfilment obligations.

nodes.id: Public Administration (Government)
nodes.label: Industry
nodes.overview: Public administration — national ministries, state/provincial agencies, and city/county/municipal governments, plus public libraries, courts, and administrative boards — is one of the most heavily and persistently targeted sectors for ransomware. Governments are attractive targets because they run large, heterogeneous, and often under-funded legacy IT estates; hold vast quantities of citizen PII and sensitive records; deliver essential, hard-to-suspend public services (911/emergency dispatch, tax and revenue collection, benefits, permitting, courts, utilities billing); and are politically visible, which raises the pressure to restore service quickly. Unlike private firms, governments frequently refuse to pay ransoms as a matter of policy — so the dominant financial exposure is not the ransom itself but the downstream cost of downtime, forensic investigation, system rebuild/replacement, credit monitoring for affected citizens, and legal/notification obligations, which routinely run many multiples of the original demand (e.g. Atlanta ~$17M vs a ~$51K demand; Baltimore ~$18M vs a ~$76K demand; Columbus $7.3M recovery vs a $1.9M demand refused). The sector also faces a distinctive blen
nodes.distinct: Large, heterogeneous, chronically under-funded legacy estates holding vast citizen PII, delivering essential services that cannot simply be suspended — 911 dispatch, tax collection, benefits, permitting, courts. Uniquely constrained on the payment decision: appropriated budgets, public-records disclosure obligations and political scrutiny mean payment is often legally or politically foreclosed, so loss migrates into extended interruption, forensic rebuild and notification cost rather than ransom. Incidents become governance and electoral events.
nodes.extortion_leverage: Disruption of essential and public-safety services combined with citizen PII exposure and acute political/reputational pressure on officials.
nodes.downtime_tolerance: Bifurcated. Near-zero for public-safety and emergency dispatch; weeks to months tolerated in practice for administrative functions, largely because recovery capacity rather than acceptable risk sets the timeline.

nodes.id: Retail Trade and Consumer Services
nodes.label: Industry
nodes.overview: Retail Trade and Consumer Services (ransomware.live's "Consumer Services" sector tag) is one of the highest-volume ransomware targeting categories, spanning everything from single-location dealerships, gyms, and jewelry shops up to multinational department-store chains, casino/hospitality operators, and the shared SaaS platforms (CRM, dealer-management systems) that underpin the industry. A live pull of the ransomware.live sector feed (~120 victim postings across roughly a 2-month window in mid-2026) shows the sector is dominated by high-volume, opportunistic ransomware-as-a-service groups (Qilin, TheGentlemen, SafePay, DragonForce, Akira, Nova, Settra) hitting mostly small/mid-size retailers, HVAC/home-services firms, funeral homes, and franchise operations, alongside a smaller number of large, named-brand victims. Layered on top of this baseline is a distinct and increasingly dominant pattern: pure data-extortion campaigns against enterprise SaaS/CRM platforms (the ShinyHunters Salesforce-vishing campaign hit Ralph Lauren, JCPenney/Catalyst Brands, and Madison Square Garden Sports Corp. in 2025-2026) that steal customer and employee data without ever deploying encryption. The sec
nodes.distinct: One of the highest-volume targeting categories, spanning single-location dealerships and gyms up to multinational chains, and dominated by high-volume opportunistic RaaS affiliates rather than targeted operators. Distinguished by extreme seasonal revenue concentration and by shared-platform concentration: dealer-management and CRM systems used across thousands of franchises mean one platform compromise produces simultaneous outages across an entire franchise network, as CDK Global demonstrated. PCI-DSS obligations and payment-card liability attach to nearly every incident.
nodes.extortion_leverage: POS and store-network outage timed to peak trading periods, plus customer payment-card and loyalty data exposure with PCI and consumer-notification consequence.
nodes.downtime_tolerance: Low. Hours to days, collapsing to near-zero during peak seasonal trading when a short outage consumes a disproportionate share of annual margin.

nodes.id: Telecommunications
nodes.label: Industry
nodes.overview: The telecommunications sector - internet service providers, mobile network operators, fixed-line/cable carriers, tower/infrastructure companies, and satellite/media-adjacent telecom firms - has become an increasingly frequent ransomware and data-extortion target. Ransomware.live's own sector tracker lists 357 telecom-sector victims (tag "Telecommunication") with a pronounced acceleration in 2025-2026 (124 posted in 2025 alone, the sector's most active year on record, plus 62 more in the first ~7 months of 2026), corroborated by Cyble/Cybersecurity Dive research showing telecom ransomware attack volume grew roughly fourfold from 24 in 2022 to 90 in 2025. The threat-actor landscape is dominated by prolific double-extortion RaaS groups (Qilin, Akira, LockBit variants, Play, Clop) alongside a newer wave of pure data-extortion/leak-only crews with no encryption capability (Arkana Security, ShinyHunters, DragonForce) that specifically target telecom's dense stores of subscriber PII, SIM/USIM credentials, and call-detail metadata. What distinguishes telecom from most other industries in this taxonomy is the sector's dual exposure: (1) a large, regulated subscriber-PII attack surface compa
nodes.distinct: 357 tracked victims with pronounced acceleration — 124 in 2025, the sector's most active year on record, plus 62 more in the first seven months of 2026. Carriers are single points of failure for downstream connectivity, so an outage propagates into every dependent business and household. Uniquely combines mass subscriber PII, core network and signaling systems functioning as OT-equivalents, and lawful-intercept and critical-infrastructure systems whose compromise carries national-security consequence beyond commercial loss.
nodes.extortion_leverage: Service availability affecting large downstream populations, plus mass subscriber PII and call-detail records with regulatory and surveillance sensitivity.
nodes.downtime_tolerance: Very low. Minutes to hours for core network and signaling; regulatory service-obligation and SLA penalties begin accruing almost immediately.

nodes.id: Transportation and Warehousing
nodes.label: Industry
nodes.overview: Transportation and Warehousing (ransomware.live sector tag "Transportation/Logistics") is a high-frequency, high-consequence ransomware target because it sits at the intersection of critical infrastructure, thin operating margins, and deeply interconnected IT/OT systems. The sector has seen some of history's costliest cyber incidents (Maersk/NotPetya, ~$300M) as well as cases where a ransomware attack directly caused a long-established company's insolvency (KNP Logistics, ~730 jobs lost). Live ransomware.live tracking shows a very high and steadily growing victim count across trucking, freight forwarding, maritime/port operators, warehousing, and fleet-technology vendors, spanning dozens of active ransomware groups and dozens of countries. Industry reporting for 2025 shows both attack frequency (+34% YoY) and average ransom demands (+685% YoY, to $2.19M) rising sharply, with third-party/supply-chain exposure (shared ELD, TMS, and port-terminal software) acting as a key amplifier — a single vendor compromise can cascade operational disruption across many otherwise-unrelated carriers simultaneously.
nodes.distinct: Sits at the intersection of critical infrastructure, thin operating margins and tightly coupled IT/OT. Produced both the costliest cyber incident on record (Maersk/NotPetya, roughly $300 million) and a documented insolvency directly caused by ransomware (KNP Logistics, roughly 730 jobs lost) — the clearest evidence that thin margins convert a survivable outage into a terminal one. Dispatch, freight and warehouse management systems have no manual fallback at modern volume.
nodes.extortion_leverage: Halted freight movement and dispatch, with cascading contractual penalties and downstream customer disruption across the shipping chain.
nodes.downtime_tolerance: Very low. Hours. Perishable and time-definite freight has effectively no tolerance, and margin structure leaves little buffer to absorb extended interruption.

nodes.id: initial access vectors
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: Initial Access Vectors
nodes.description: How ransomware actors most commonly gain a foothold in transportation/warehousing environments, shaped by the industry's mix of legacy OT, distributed fleet/warehouse sites, and often-thin IT security staffing relative to operational scale.

nodes.id: extortion tactics
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: Extortion Tactics
nodes.description: The specific leverage mechanisms ransomware groups use against transportation/logistics targets, reflecting a broader industry shift toward data theft and multi-pronged pressure over pure encryption.

nodes.id: operational technology ot and physical safety adjacent risk
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: Operational technology (OT) and physical-safety-adjacent risk
nodes.description: Unlike pure back-office IT sectors, hospitality/entertainment venues integrate IT with physical operations, so a ransomware event can directly disrupt guest safety, access, and physical service delivery, not just data confidentiality.

nodes.id: third party and supply chain risk
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: Third-Party / Supply-Chain Risk
nodes.description: Because logistics networks are inherently interconnected, an attack on one node (a carrier, a software vendor, a port) propagates operational and reputational damage across partners and customers.

nodes.id: insider and workforce risk
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: Insider & Workforce Risk
nodes.description: Distributed, high-turnover workforces (drivers, warehouse staff, seasonal labor) and thin security-awareness investment create human-factor exposure distinct from office-centric industries.

nodes.id: regulatory contractual and reputational exposure
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: Regulatory, contractual and reputational exposure
nodes.description: Data-protection, payment-card, and consumer-protection obligations that shape breach costs and downstream liability specific to guest-data-heavy businesses.

nodes.id: extortion and impact tactics
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: Extortion & Impact Tactics
nodes.description: The mix of leverage attackers apply. In this sector the physical perishability and food-security angle amplifies pressure to pay quickly.

nodes.id: ot ics and physical process risk
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: OT / ICS & Physical-Process Risk
nodes.description: Operational-technology exposure specific to farms and food plants where cyber impact becomes physical and food-safety relevant.

nodes.id: supply chain and third party concentration risk
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: Supply-Chain & Third-Party Concentration Risk
nodes.description: The sector's consolidation and just-in-time structure mean one victim's outage propagates widely; conversely, victims are exposed through their many upstream vendors.

nodes.id: regulatory legal and food security exposure
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: Regulatory, Legal & Food-Security Exposure
nodes.description: Compliance and liability hazards triggered by an incident, heightened by critical-infrastructure designation and personal-data holdings.

nodes.id: insider workforce and operational maturity risk
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: Insider, Workforce & Operational-Maturity Risk
nodes.description: Human and organizational weaknesses characteristic of the sector.

nodes.id: ot iot and jobsite facilities technology risk
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: OT, IoT and Jobsite/Facilities Technology Risk
nodes.description: Physical and operational-technology exposure distinct to construction and post-construction facilities management, generally less targeted today than pure-IT systems but a growing concern.

nodes.id: regulatory and legal exposure
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: Regulatory & Legal Exposure
nodes.description: Telecom's status as a heavily regulated, often critical-infrastructure-designated sector amplifies post-incident financial and legal consequences beyond the ransom/attack itself.

nodes.id: business interruption project delay risk
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: Business Interruption / Project Delay Risk
nodes.description: How ransomware translates into operational and financial disruption specific to project-based construction work.

nodes.id: initial access via open and federated campus environments
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: Initial Access via Open and Federated Campus Environments
nodes.description: Education networks are architecturally adversarial to containment. Universities operate deliberately open networks supporting public research collaboration, guest access, self-managed student devices and thousands of transient accounts per year, while K-12 districts run flat networks with minimal segmentation and small IT teams. Sophos found exploited vulnerabilities to be the single largest root cause in higher education (35% of attacks) and phishing the leading cause in lower education (22%), reflecting the two different failure modes. Verizon DBIR data has repeatedly placed social engineering and system intrusion as the dominant education breach patterns.

nodes.id: extortion leverage from minors and student data
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: Extortion Leverage from Minors' and Student Data
nodes.description: Education is uniquely coercible because the hostage data belongs largely to children. Actors have moved from encryption-first to exfiltration-led extortion and apply pressure through channels unavailable in other sectors: publishing psychological evaluations, special-education records and abuse reports, and contacting students and parents directly. In the LAUSD and Minneapolis cases the leaked corpora included student psychological assessments, and in Minneapolis campus security blueprints - creating physical-safety as well as privacy harm. Sophos recorded extortion-only (no encryption) attacks rising in both education strata.

nodes.id: third party and edtech vendor concentration risk
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: Third-Party and Edtech Vendor Concentration Risk
nodes.description: The single most severe systemic hazard in the sector. A handful of SIS, LMS and assessment platforms serve most of the addressable market, so one vendor intrusion becomes a correlated loss across thousands of insureds simultaneously. PowerSchool (Dec 2024) reached a claimed 62.4 million students and 9.5 million teachers across approximately 6,505 districts from one compromised credential; Instructure/Canvas (May 2026) was claimed to affect 275 million users across roughly 9,000 institutions. Verizon's 2026 DBIR reported third-party involvement in 48% of breaches with supply-chain breaches up 60%. For a cyber-insurance portfolio this is the dominant aggregation exposure in the education book.

nodes.id: insider and student originated threat
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: Insider and Student-Originated Threat
nodes.description: Education is the rare sector in which a substantial share of the resident population is both technically capable and directly motivated to attack the institution's systems - for grade alteration, exam access or reputational reasons - while holding legitimate network credentials. The PowerSchool intrusion was ultimately attributed by the US DOJ to a 19-year-old university student, who pleaded guilty. Insider events blur the ransomware/fraud boundary and complicate coverage triggers.

nodes.id: regulatory notification and litigation exposure
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: Regulatory, Notification and Litigation Exposure
nodes.description: Education carries a dense, overlapping and unusually child-focused compliance regime, so a single ransomware event generates parallel regulatory tracks. FERPA and COPPA apply federally in the US, layered with state student-privacy statutes and state breach laws; UK and EU institutions face UK GDPR/GDPR and ICO scrutiny; universities holding clinical or research-health data additionally trigger HIPAA. Notification is frequently slow - Minneapolis took seven months to notify 105,617 people, and the University of Hawai'i Cancer Center's delay in notifying study participants drew specific criticism - which compounds regulatory and class-action risk.

nodes.id: operational disruption of instruction and institutional continuity
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: Operational Disruption of Instruction and Institutional Continuity
nodes.description: Unlike most commercial insureds, schools cannot fail over to a degraded manual mode: an encrypted district frequently closes entirely. Highline Public Schools shut all 34 schools for three days; the British Library's core services were disrupted for months. Comparitech measured an average of 10.7 days of downtime per education incident, peaking at 12.6 days in 2023. Lost instructional days carry statutory make-up obligations, transport and meal-programme knock-ons, and in higher education can delay terms, research grants and graduation.

nodes.id: underfunded security posture and recovery capability
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: Underfunded Security Posture and Recovery Capability
nodes.description: The sector's loss severity is driven less by attacker sophistication than by chronic under-resourcing. Sophos found lack of expertise and limited incident-response capacity cited by 42% each in lower education, and 49% of higher education institutions citing unknown security gaps. Backup reliability has degraded: recovery from backups fell to 59% in lower education and 47% in higher education. Public institutions face procurement cycles, capital-budget constraints and elected-board approval that slow both hardening and response.

nodes.id: ot vs it risk cyber physical
nodes.label: Hazard
nodes.name: OT vs IT Risk (Cyber-Physical)
nodes.description: The defining hazard of this sector: the interface between enterprise IT and operational technology (ICS/SCADA/DCS) controlling physical energy flows. IT-only ransomware routinely forces OT shutdowns, and OT-capable malware threatens physical damage.

nodes.id: regulatory legal and reputational exposure

nodes.description: Energy is heavily regulated as critical infrastructure; incidents trigger mandatory reporting, sanctions-screening on ransom payment, and public/political scrutiny.

nodes.id: student information systems sis and core records
nodes.label: Exposure
nodes.name: Student Information Systems (SIS) and Core Records
nodes.description: The system of record for enrolment, demographics, attendance, discipline and transcripts, and the highest-value single target in education because it concentrates minors' PII for an entire district or institution in one platform. SIS compromise is both a direct exposure at the institution and, via the vendor, the sector's principal aggregation event - the PowerSchool intrusion reached a claimed 62.4 million students and 9.5 million teachers across approximately 6,505 districts.

nodes.id: learning management systems gradebooks and instructional platforms
nodes.label: Exposure
nodes.name: Learning Management Systems, Gradebooks and Instructional Platforms
nodes.description: The day-to-day instructional layer - LMS, gradebook, courseware, assessment and proctoring tools. Outage halts teaching directly, and the platforms hold years of coursework, private messaging and behavioural data. The May 2026 Instructure/Canvas incident demonstrated the scale: attackers claimed 3.6TB covering 275 million users across roughly 9,000 institutions, including private student-teacher messages, in a platform used by 41% of US higher education institutions.

nodes.id: financial aid bursar payroll and payment systems
nodes.label: Exposure
nodes.name: Financial Aid, Bursar, Payroll and Payment Systems
nodes.description: Education institutions process tuition, financial aid, donations, payroll and vendor payments, and financial-aid files in particular concentrate exactly the identity elements needed for fraud - SSNs, bank details and full household income data (FAFSA). Encryption here halts payroll and disbursement; exfiltration produces the sector's highest per-record identity-theft severity.

nodes.id: research data intellectual property and regulated research health data
nodes.label: Exposure
nodes.name: Research Data, Intellectual Property and Regulated Research Health Data
nodes.description: The exposure unique to higher education. Universities hold pre-publication research, proprietary and licensed datasets, export-controlled work and long-running human-subjects cohorts. The University of Manchester attack reached NHS records for 1.1 million patients gathered from over 200 hospitals for medical research, and the University of Hawai'i Cancer Center incident exposed decades-old epidemiological cohort data affecting up to 1.15 million individuals - demonstrating that research archives create liability for populations who were never students or staff.

nodes.id: minors pii and sensitive student welfare records
nodes.label: Exposure
nodes.name: Minors' PII and Sensitive Student Welfare Records
nodes.description: The sector's most reputationally and legally explosive exposure. Beyond routine PII, schools hold counselling notes, psychological evaluations, abuse and safeguarding reports, and custody arrangements for children who cannot consent and whose identities remain exploitable for decades. Both LAUSD and Minneapolis saw student psychological assessments published after refusing to pay, and Baltimore City Public Schools' 2025 incident exposed SSNs and driver's licence data for thousands of students and staff.

nodes.id: campus operational technology and physical safety systems
nodes.label: Exposure
nodes.name: Campus Operational Technology and Physical Safety Systems
nodes.description: Schools and campuses run building and safety infrastructure on the same networks as administrative IT, so ransomware translates directly into physical-safety consequences and closure decisions. The Minneapolis breach was confirmed by analysts to have exposed school security blueprints - a worst-case outcome in which stolen data creates ongoing physical risk to children that no notification or credit monitoring can remediate.

nodes.id: alumni donor and advancement databases
nodes.label: Exposure
nodes.name: Alumni, Donor and Advancement Databases
nodes.description: University advancement systems hold high-net-worth individuals' financial profiles, giving histories, wealth-screening assessments and private correspondence. This data is disproportionately valuable relative to its volume, and its exposure damages the institution's fundraising capacity - a material revenue line for higher education - well beyond the incident itself. The University of Manchester breach included alumni records alongside current student data.
