nodes.id: Accommodation, Food Services, Arts and Entertainment::MGM Resorts International
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: MGM disclosed an estimated ~$100 million negative impact to Adjusted Property EBITDAR for Las Vegas Strip and Regional Operations, plus under $10 million in one-time remediation/legal/incident-response costs; company said it expected to be largely covered by cyber insurance. A related shareholder/consumer class-action settlement was reached in 2025.
nodes.ransom: MGM has stated it did not pay a ransom (unlike sister-incident Caesars); no confirmed dollar figure for a demand specific to MGM has been publicly disclosed.
nodes.downtime: Core systems (slot machines, digital key cards, reservations, payment processing) were down for approximately 10 days before full restoration.
nodes.data_impact: Personal information (names, contact details, driver's license/SSN/passport numbers for some) of roughly 37 million MGM Rewards members was compromised.
nodes.summary: Scattered Spider used a vishing/social-engineering attack against MGM's IT help desk to obtain credentials, then deployed ALPHV/BlackCat ransomware, forcing MGM to shut down casino floor systems, digital hotel room keys, slot machines, ATMs, restaurant/payment systems and websites across 30+ properties for roughly 10 days.

nodes.id: Accommodation, Food Services, Arts and Entertainment::Caesars Entertainment
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Caesars disclosed the incident in an SEC 8-K; ongoing consumer class-action litigation (Caesars Entertainment Data Breach Litigation). Specific total incident cost beyond the ransom payment not publicly broken out.
nodes.ransom: Attackers initially demanded $30 million; Caesars paid approximately $15 million in cryptocurrency. The FBI later tracked and froze a portion of the payment as it moved through crypto exchanges.
nodes.downtime: Caesars stated its hotel, casino and online operations were not significantly disrupted (unlike MGM); recovery was largely on the data-breach/notification track rather than an operational-outage track.
nodes.data_impact: Loyalty program database of more than 65 million Caesars Rewards members exposed, including driver's license and Social Security numbers for a subset of members.
nodes.summary: Attackers compromised a third-party IT support vendor via social engineering to breach Caesars' network and exfiltrate the ~6TB Caesars Rewards loyalty database before Caesars negotiated and paid a ransom; the attack occurred just before, and is closely associated with, the MGM incident by the same threat-actor ecosystem.

nodes.id: Accommodation, Food Services, Arts and Entertainment::Carnival Corporation & plc
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.date: April 2026 (initial access April 14; discovered/blocked April 22; disclosed publicly ~mid-May 2026)
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as a specific dollar figure by Carnival; the company began offering two years of complimentary TransUnion credit monitoring to affected US residents, an ongoing cost. Litigation/regulatory exposure likely given the scale of records.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed; ShinyHunters is an extortion-focused (data-theft, not necessarily encryption) group and threatened to publish/sell the data if terms were not met.
nodes.downtime: No major operational/cruise-booking outage reported; this was primarily a data-theft/social-engineering incident rather than an encryption/downtime event.
nodes.data_impact: Data breach notice filed in Maine listed 5,995,277 affected individuals; ShinyHunters claimed 8.7 million records stolen. Exposed data included names, addresses, emails, phone numbers, dates of birth, and government ID numbers (driver's license, passport).
nodes.summary: ShinyHunters used social engineering to trick a Carnival employee into granting IT system access, then used the compromised account to copy personal data from a limited portion of Carnival's systems before being blocked; the gang later claimed 8.7 million stolen records and published data on its leak site.

nodes.id: Accommodation, Food Services, Arts and Entertainment::Compass Group Australia (Sydney-based catering/support services group)
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.victim: Compass Group Australia (Sydney-based catering/support services group)
nodes.date: September 2024 (first attack disclosed Sept 4; second Medusa-affiliate attack later in September, data posted Sept 18, 2024)
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed by Compass Group; company activated its incident response plan and notified employees, clients, suppliers and regulators.
nodes.ransom: First attack: Medusa demanded US$2 million to delete/not publish the ~785.5GB of stolen data (with a US$100,000/day deadline-extension fee). Second (separate) attack: ransom demanded was US$100,000. Not publicly confirmed whether any payment was made.
nodes.downtime: Specific downtime duration not publicly detailed in press coverage; company stated it secured systems and launched an investigation with external cybersecurity specialists.
nodes.data_impact: Near 1TB combined across both incidents; data included employee wage declarations and scanned passports/driver's licenses of contractors and staff, with the threat actor threatening publication on its dark-web leak site.
nodes.summary: Medusa ransomware affiliates breached Compass Group's Australian IT network twice within the same month, exfiltrating close to 1TB of data combined, including employee wage records and scanned passports/driver's licenses of contractors, then threatened publication on Medusa's leak site.

nodes.id: Accommodation, Food Services, Arts and Entertainment::Panera Bread
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.date: March 2024 (outage began March 22, resolved around March 26, 2024)
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed by Panera; the company did not release financial figures. Independent security analysts estimated such multi-day enterprise ransomware disruptions typically cost tens of millions of dollars in lost sales and recovery, but no Panera-specific figure has been confirmed.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed; no group claimed responsibility and Panera did not comment on any ransom demand or payment.
nodes.downtime: Approximately one week (March 22-26, 2024) of major IT outage across point-of-sale, online ordering, loyalty and phone systems before restoration.
nodes.data_impact: A subsequent notice confirmed an employee data breach tied to the March incident (SSNs and other employee personal data); customer payment-data exposure was not confirmed.
nodes.summary: A ransomware attack encrypted numerous Panera Bread virtual machines, taking down point-of-sale systems, online/mobile ordering, the loyalty (MyPanera) program, and internal phone systems across the chain's roughly 2,160 cafés; stores stayed open but had to fall back to cash-only transactions during the outage.

nodes.id: Accommodation, Food Services, Arts and Entertainment::Nordic Choice Hotels
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.country: Norway/Scandinavia (200 properties across Scandinavia, Finland, and the Baltics)
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as a specific dollar figure.
nodes.ransom: Nordic Choice stated it deliberately did not contact Conti and had not received (or did not intend to pay) a ransom demand; no payment reported.
nodes.downtime: Replacement/workaround solutions were in place at most hotels within days of the attack (over the following weekend), with normal operations restored within about a week.
nodes.data_impact: Guest booking data and Nordic Choice Club (loyalty) member data were confirmed potentially exposed; no indication passwords or payment card data were affected.
nodes.summary: Conti ransomware hit Nordic Choice Hotels' central IT systems, disabling reservation, check-in/check-out, room key-card and payment systems across its ~200-property, 16,000-employee hotel network; staff fell back to manual processes while replacement systems were rolled out property-by-property.

nodes.id: Accommodation, Food Services, Arts and Entertainment::Rivers Casino Des Plaines / Rush Street Gaming
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.victim: Rivers Casino Des Plaines / Rush Street Gaming
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed; the casino faced a class-action lawsuit over the data breach.
nodes.ransom: For the 2025 Rivers Casino Philadelphia/Rush Street Gaming Cicada3301 claim, an undisclosed ransom was demanded with a stated deadline (Feb 15, 2025); no payment publicly confirmed. No ransom figure disclosed for the 2023 Illinois breach.
nodes.downtime: No major operational outage publicly reported; this was primarily a data-theft/notification incident rather than an encryption/downtime event.
nodes.data_impact: Names, birth dates, contact info, driver's license/government ID numbers, Social Security numbers, bank account and tax ID information, and passport numbers for a subset of customers and employees (at least 8,151 individuals per Comparitech); the 2025 Cicada3301 claim alleged 2.56TB of data stolen from Rush Street Gaming.
nodes.summary: Hackers accessed files containing personal data of customers and employees at Rivers Casino (Illinois); the breach was discovered months after the intrusion, leading to consumer notification, class-action litigation, and a separate 2025 Cicada3301 extortion claim against the related Rivers Casino Philadelphia/Rush Street Gaming entity.

nodes.id: Accommodation, Food Services, Arts and Entertainment::Disneyland Paris
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.date: June 2025 (claimed on leak site June 20, 2025; group teased on social media June 12)
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed; Disneyland Paris had not acknowledged the breach in public statements found.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed/unclear whether a ransom was demanded of Disneyland Paris directly versus its partner firm.
nodes.downtime: No park operational disruption reported; this was a third-party/supply-chain data-exposure incident rather than an IT outage at the park itself.
nodes.data_impact: Approximately 64GB / ~39,000 files of construction and renovation-related documents and media allegedly exposed via a Disneyland partner company, not confirmed to include guest personal data.
nodes.summary: Anubis ransomware claimed the largest data leak in Disneyland Paris's history, alleging the data (obtained via breach of a construction/renovation partner company rather than Disneyland directly) included ~39,000 files of park construction and renovation plans, exposing images/videos of attraction designs (Crush's Coaster, Frozen, Ratatouille, Buzz Lightyear, Phantom Manor, etc.). Disneyland Paris had not publicly confirmed the claims as of the reporting.

nodes.id: Accommodation, Food Services, Arts and Entertainment::Inspired Entertainment, Inc.
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: not publicly disclosed
nodes.ransom: not publicly disclosed
nodes.downtime: The affected IT systems have now been substantially restored to full operational capabilities.
nodes.data_impact: Company data, including personal data, was exfiltrated.
nodes.summary: On November 8, 2023, Inspired Entertainment, Inc. detected a ransomware attack that disrupted its corporate IT systems. The company initiated response protocols and engaged cybersecurity experts, later discovering that personal data had been exfiltrated on November 15, 2023.

nodes.id: Accommodation, Food Services, Arts and Entertainment::Yum! Brands, Inc.
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: not publicly disclosed
nodes.ransom: not publicly disclosed
nodes.downtime: Less than 300 restaurants in the United Kingdom were closed for one day; all stores are now operational and systems are expected to be largely restored in the coming days.
nodes.data_impact: Data was taken from the Company's network; no evidence that customer databases were stolen.
nodes.summary: On January 18, 2023, Yum! Brands, Inc. announced a ransomware attack that impacted certain information technology systems. The company initiated response protocols and engaged cybersecurity professionals, while confirming that less than 300 restaurants in the UK were temporarily closed but are now operational.

nodes.id: Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Food Production::JBS S.A. / JBS USA
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Direct operational disruption to global meat supply; JBS did not publicly quantify total losses beyond the ransom. Widely cited as one of the most consequential critical-infrastructure attacks of 2021.
nodes.ransom: REvil initially demanded $22.5 million; JBS negotiated and paid $11 million in Bitcoin.
nodes.downtime: Multiple North American and Australian plants shut for roughly a day-plus; JBS said the majority of facilities were operational again within days, choosing to pay to avoid prolonged disruption and possible data exfiltration.
nodes.data_impact: JBS said it paid partly to ensure no data was exfiltrated; no large-scale data leak was confirmed at the time.
nodes.summary: The world's largest meat processor was hit by REvil, forcing shutdown of beef and pork slaughterhouses across the US, Canada and Australia and disrupting roughly a fifth of US meat capacity. Internal DHS records later characterized JBS's pre-attack cybersecurity as unusually poor. Ransomware.live also tracks a later 2026 'coinbasecartel' posting recycling ~3TB of JBS data, illustrating re-extortion.

nodes.id: Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Food Production::United Natural Foods, Inc. (UNFI)
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Estimated $350–$400 million reduction in fiscal-2025 net sales; net income impact of $50–$60 million and adjusted EBITDA impact of ~$40–$50 million. Included ~$20 million in manual-workaround costs and ~$5 million in remediation. Company said it expects insurance proceeds to be adequate to substantially offset losses.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.downtime: Systems taken offline in early June 2025; company ran manual workarounds and said the operational impact was mostly contained to the quarter, with phased restoration over subsequent weeks.
nodes.data_impact: Not detailed publicly; impact framed primarily as operational/supply disruption.
nodes.summary: North America's largest grocery distributor and primary supplier to Whole Foods was forced to take core systems offline after a June 2025 cyberattack, crippling electronic ordering and invoicing across its 53 distribution centers serving 30,000+ retail locations and emptying shelves nationwide. One of the largest quantified financial hits in the sector.

nodes.id: Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Food Production::Dole plc (Dole Food Company)
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Total incident impact of $10.5 million for the quarter ended March 31, 2023 (of which $4.8 million related to continuing operations); CEO warned the financial impact would not be fully recoverable through insurance.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.downtime: North American operations briefly shut down; most disruptive to Fresh Vegetables and Chilean businesses. All impacted servers and end-user computers were subsequently restored or rebuilt with third-party IR support.
nodes.data_impact: Dole later disclosed the attack breached data of almost 3,900 US workers.
nodes.summary: One of the world's largest fresh-produce suppliers suffered a February 2023 ransomware attack that hit about half of Legacy Dole's servers and a quarter of end-user computers, briefly shutting North American operations and causing widely reported packaged-salad shortages on US store shelves.

nodes.id: Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Food Production::Ahold Delhaize USA (Giant Food, Hannaford, Food Lion, Stop & Shop, The Giant Company)
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.victim: Ahold Delhaize USA (Giant Food, Hannaford, Food Lion, Stop & Shop, The Giant Company)
nodes.financial_impact: Not separately quantified in dollar terms publicly; costs include breach response and two years of free credit monitoring/identity protection for 2.24M affected individuals.
nodes.ransom: No ransom reported paid — attackers published ~800GB of data on their leak site, indicating non-payment.
nodes.downtime: Network issues across US pharmacies and supermarkets in November 2024; systems restored over following weeks.
nodes.data_impact: Breach affected 2,242,521 people; leaked data included names, postal/email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth and government IDs (SSNs, driver's licenses, passports).
nodes.summary: The US division of the multinational grocery/food retailer detected unauthorized access on Nov 6, 2024, disrupting pharmacies and supermarket network systems. INC Ransom claimed the attack in April 2025, asserting up to 6TB of stolen data; the incident became one of the largest food-retail data breaches on record.

nodes.id: Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Food Production::NEW Cooperative Inc.
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed; the co-op proactively took systems offline to contain impact rather than pay.
nodes.ransom: BlackMatter demanded $5.9 million, escalating to $11.8 million if unpaid within five days. Reporting indicated the co-op did not pay.
nodes.downtime: Systems taken offline proactively to contain the threat; operations managed via workarounds while remediation proceeded with law enforcement and security experts.
nodes.data_impact: BlackMatter claimed theft of financial information, HR data, R&D information and source code for the 'SoilMap' agricultural technology platform.
nodes.summary: An Iowa farm cooperative providing feed, grain and crop-protection services was hit by BlackMatter, which locked systems used to manage food supply chains and animal-feeding schedules. The co-op said ~40% of US grain production runs through its software and warned the attack could 'break the supply chain very shortly,' making it a landmark food-security incident.

nodes.id: Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Food Production::KP Snacks
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed; disruption to order processing and distribution for roughly two months with supply-chain knock-on to retailers.
nodes.ransom: Conti operated double-extortion with a leak-site countdown; ransom amount and any payment not publicly confirmed.
nodes.downtime: Order placement and delivery disrupted from late January with no normal service expected until at least end of March 2022.
nodes.data_impact: Conti published samples including credit-card statements, birth certificates, and spreadsheets with employee addresses and phone numbers on its leak site.
nodes.summary: The UK snack maker (Hula Hoops, McCoy's, KP Nuts, Tyrrells, Butterkist) discovered a Conti ransomware attack on Jan 28, 2022 that disrupted IT systems so severely it could not safely process orders or dispatch goods, prompting warnings of crisp and snack shortages through at least March.

nodes.id: Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Food Production::Maple Leaf Foods
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Company acknowledged the outage would cause operational and financial impact and expected full resolution to take time; specific loss figure not itemized publicly.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed; Maple Leaf publicly indicated it would not accede to criminal demands.
nodes.downtime: System outage began early November 2022 with recovery efforts extending over subsequent weeks while the company used workarounds to maintain supply.
nodes.data_impact: Not detailed publicly at scale; primarily an operational-disruption event.
nodes.summary: One of Canada's largest packaged-meats and food producers suffered a November 2022 outage attributed to Black Basta ransomware, causing a system disruption that affected operations and order fulfillment across its network; recorded in the ransomware.live sector dataset as a Black Basta victim.

nodes.id: Construction::Ferrovial
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed; no company financial statement or disclosed cost found.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.downtime: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.data_impact: Per HudsonRock infostealer telemetry referenced on the incident's ransomware.live page: 147 compromised employee accounts, 16 compromised user accounts, 106 third-party employee credentials, and 27 external attack-surface exposures identified. Underlying stolen data types/volume from the ransomware group's own leak were not detailed in available sources as of this writing (incident is very recent/
nodes.summary: AiLock, a double-extortion RaaS group active since March 2025, claimed Ferrovial - a global infrastructure and mobility operator involved in construction and design plus toll-road concessions - on its leak site. AiLock's model gives victims a 72-hour response window and up to five days to pay, threatening regulator notification and competitor disclosure if unpaid.

nodes.id: Construction::Balfour Beatty
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.date: October 12, 2025 and April 8, 2026 (two separate claimed incidents)
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed for either incident.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed for either incident.
nodes.downtime: Not publicly disclosed for either incident.
nodes.data_impact: Leak size described as 'unknown' in available secondary reporting for both incidents; no confirmed data-type breakdown found in public sources.
nodes.summary: Balfour Beatty, a leading UK-headquartered international infrastructure group delivering construction, engineering and support services across transportation, power, buildings and civil works in the UK, US and other markets, was claimed by two different ransomware groups within a six-month span: INC Ransom in October 2025 (targeting US operations) and CoinbaseCartel in April 2026 (UK).

nodes.id: Construction::Bechtel Corporation
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.country: United States (privately held, one of the world's largest engineering/construction/project-management firms, major US government contractor)
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed by Bechtel; no company statement located.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.downtime: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.data_impact: Specific data types/volume exfiltrated from Bechtel were not detailed in available sources; the broader Oracle EBS campaign is understood to have exposed enterprise financial, HR and procurement data (the standard EBS module set) at affected organizations generally.
nodes.summary: Bechtel was named by the Clop ransomware group as part of a large-scale extortion wave exploiting a zero-day vulnerability (CVE-2025-61882) in Oracle E-Business Suite. Clop posted roughly 39 victim organizations across many industries within a 24-hour window in this campaign; Clop had earlier exfiltrated data via the Oracle EBS flaw in August 2025 and followed up with mass extortion emails in late September 2025 before publishing leak-site listings in November.

nodes.id: Construction::Kier Group plc (KIER.CO.UK)
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.country: United Kingdom (major listed construction, property and infrastructure services company, LSE:KIE)
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed; Clop threatened to release data absent negotiation.
nodes.downtime: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.data_impact: Per secondary reporting citing infostealer-derived telemetry on the incident record: 4 employees, 120 users, and 23 third-party employee credentials referenced as compromised/exposed; specific stolen-file categories from the Clop leak itself were not detailed in available sources.
nodes.summary: Kier Group, a leading UK construction, civil-engineering, property and infrastructure services company operating across defence, transportation, health, education and utilities, was claimed by Clop as part of the same Oracle E-Business Suite CVE-2025-61882 mass-exploitation campaign that hit Bechtel days later.

nodes.id: Construction::Kajima Europe
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.country: United Kingdom / continental Europe operations of Kajima Corporation (Japan, one of the world's largest construction firms)
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.downtime: Not publicly disclosed/documented in available sources.
nodes.data_impact: Approximately 400 GB of data reported exfiltrated, including engineering documents, CAD designs and blueprints, financial and investment records, construction contracts and procurement documentation, internal communications, subcontractor lists and payment schedules, employee HR files/credentials, and project-management files.
nodes.summary: Qilin, one of the most prolific ransomware groups globally in 2025 (claiming roughly 800 victims across 50+ countries since January 2025, and dominant in Europe with 65 Q3-2025 victims per Cyble), claimed Kajima Europe, the European arm of major Japanese construction group Kajima Corporation, exfiltrating a large volume of corporate and project data.

nodes.id: Construction::AECOM
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.country: United States (Fortune 500 global engineering, design and infrastructure-consulting firm)
nodes.financial_impact: Specific incident-response, remediation or credit-monitoring costs were not publicly disclosed; no stock-impact or insurance-payout figures found in public sources.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.downtime: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.data_impact: Personal information of present and former AECOM employees was exposed, including names, addresses, Social Security numbers, and personal bank account and routing numbers, via compromise of the US payroll system; exact number of employees affected was not confirmed in available public sources.
nodes.summary: AECOM was compromised in a payroll-system hack attributed to the Pysa (Mespinoza) ransomware group's double-extortion operators; AECOM subsequently notified current and former employees that their personal data had been exposed and reported the incident to the California Attorney General's office. This is one of the better-documented incidents in the sector because it produced a formal breach notification rather than only a leak-site claim.

nodes.id: Construction::Turner Construction Company
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.country: United States (one of the largest construction management firms in the US)
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.downtime: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.data_impact: Specific data types/volume were not detailed in available public sources beyond the leak-site listing itself.
nodes.summary: Turner Construction Company was listed as a victim by the Everest ransomware group, a double-extortion (and increasingly pure data-extortion) operator active since December 2020 that has targeted government, healthcare, manufacturing and IT-services organizations across North America, Europe and Asia. Turner's inclusion illustrates the group's willingness to target top-tier construction management firms.

nodes.id: Educational Services::PowerSchool (SIS vendor serving K-12 districts in the US, Canada and elsewhere)
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.victim: PowerSchool (SIS vendor serving K-12 districts in the US, Canada and elsewhere)
nodes.financial_impact: Total programme cost not publicly disclosed. PowerSchool offered two years of identity protection and credit monitoring to affected students and educators; class-action litigation followed. Individual district remediation and notification costs were not publicly itemised.
nodes.ransom: Approximately $2.85 million in bitcoin demanded and PAID by PowerSchool, per US Department of Justice court documents made public 20 May 2025. Amounts sought in the subsequent district-level extortion attempts were not publicly disclosed.
nodes.downtime: No mass encryption event - this was exfiltration-only extortion, so districts did not suffer the closure pattern typical of encryption attacks. Recovery centred on notification, credit monitoring, credential resets and multi-jurisdiction regulatory response, extending well beyond a year and reopening when re-extortion began in May 2025.
nodes.data_impact: The attacker claimed data on 62.4 million students and 9.5 million teachers across approximately 6,505 school districts in the US, Canada and other countries. Exposed fields included names, addresses, dates of birth, contact details, and for some individuals Social Security numbers and medical/grade information. Affected populations are overwhelmingly minors, whose identity exposure persists for d
nodes.summary: The defining edtech aggregation event. An attacker used compromised credentials to access PowerSchool's PowerSource support portal and exfiltrate student and teacher data from the hosted SIS environment. PowerSchool paid an extortion demand in exchange for a video purporting to show deletion of the only copy of the data. The deletion proved worthless: in May 2025 the same data was used to extort individual school districts directly in Canada and North Carolina, with attackers sending samples to schools. PowerSchool stated it did not believe this was a new intrusion because the samples matched the December theft. This is the clearest available demonstration that paying for a deletion promise transfers no risk downstream, and that a single vendor compromise generates thousands of correlated district-level losses.

nodes.id: Educational Services::Instructure Holdings, Inc. (Canvas LMS)
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.date: 2026-05-01 (intrusion 29-30 April 2026; second breach within roughly two weeks)
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed. Institutional costs spanned incident response, forensic review, portal remediation after defacement, and notification across thousands of schools.
nodes.ransom: Ransom PAID by Instructure under an agreement reached 11 May 2026; the amount was not publicly disclosed. Attackers reportedly returned the data and supplied 'shred logs' as claimed proof of destruction - the same unverifiable deletion assurance seen in the PowerSchool case.
nodes.downtime: Instructure took Canvas, Canvas Beta and Canvas Test offline on 7 May 2026 for investigation and restored service the following day; Canvas Data 2 and Canvas Beta had been in maintenance since 1 May. The Free-For-Teacher account programme was permanently shut down as a remediation measure. Roughly 330 institutions additionally had to remediate defaced login portals.
nodes.data_impact: ShinyHunters claimed 3.6TB covering 275 million users across approximately 9,000 institutions (reporting also cites 8,809 universities, education ministries and other bodies) - figures Instructure has not confirmed. Instructure confirmed exposure of names, email addresses, student ID numbers and some private messages between Canvas users, and stated there was no evidence that passwords, financial
nodes.summary: Described in reporting as the largest education-sector breach on record. ShinyHunters exploited Instructure's Free-For-Teacher (FFT) programme - which allowed educators to create Canvas accounts without institutional verification - to reach production data, then breached the platform a second time within about two weeks. After Instructure missed the initial 7 May negotiation deadline, the group escalated by defacing Canvas login portals at roughly 330 institutions and pivoting to direct school-by-school extortion with a final 12 May deadline. Instructure reached a payment agreement on 11 May, one day before the leak deadline. The incident is the purest example of LMS vendor concentration risk: Canvas is used by 41% of US higher education institutions, so a single platform intrusion simultaneously exposed thousands of otherwise unconnected insureds.

nodes.id: Educational Services::University of Hawai'i Cancer Center
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed. Costs included ransom payment, third-party forensic and recovery support, and notification plus remediation for up to 1.15 million individuals.
nodes.ransom: Ransom PAID - the centre worked with third-party cybersecurity experts to obtain a decryption tool and paid to prevent publication of the stolen data. The amount was not publicly disclosed.
nodes.downtime: Encrypted data was recovered using a decryption tool obtained through the payment. Specific outage duration was not publicly disclosed. Notification lagged roughly four months behind discovery, with the centre compiling names and addresses for study participants well after the August 2025 intrusion.
nodes.data_impact: Up to 1.15 million individuals affected (some reporting cites approximately 1.2 million). Exposed data included Social Security numbers and driver's licence numbers sourced from the Hawai'i State Department of Transportation, and City and County of Honolulu voter registration records from 1998. Much of the affected population were research study participants rather than students or employees.
nodes.summary: A university research-archive breach that illustrates how higher education accumulates liability for populations who were never students or staff. Attackers reached data from the Multiethnic Cohort (MEC) Study, a longitudinal epidemiological study established in 1993, plus files from three other diet-and-cancer studies. Compounding the event, the university did not notify affected study participants for roughly four months - a delay that drew specific public criticism and independent regulatory risk. Notably, the university PAID to prevent publication, making this one of the few education cases with a confirmed payment decision.

nodes.id: Educational Services::Highline Public Schools
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed. Costs included district-wide re-imaging of all student and staff devices, third-party forensic engagement, and three days of lost instruction across 34 schools.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed - the district declined to say how much was demanded, citing the ongoing investigation, and did not publicly confirm any payment.
nodes.downtime: All schools and activities closed for three days, from Monday 9 September through Wednesday 11 September 2024, reopening Thursday 12 September. Network systems remained disrupted into October 2024, when all student and staff devices had been re-imaged - roughly a month of degraded operation after classes resumed.
nodes.data_impact: The district confirmed that highly sensitive personal, financial and medical data was breached. The precise number of affected students and staff was not publicly disclosed in the reporting reviewed.
nodes.summary: The canonical K-12 operational-disruption case. Highline, a Washington state district of 34 schools serving roughly 17,500 students and 2,000 staff, detected the intrusion on a Saturday and immediately isolated critical systems - then closed every school and all activities for three days because core instructional and safety systems could not be trusted. It demonstrates the sector's defining characteristic for insurers: a school district has no degraded operating mode, so business interruption manifests as total closure of an essential public service, with statutory make-up obligations and knock-on effects to transport and meal programmes.

nodes.id: Educational Services::British Library
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Approximately GBP 6-7 million in recovery costs, funded from roughly 40% of the library's financial reserves - about ten times the ransom demanded.
nodes.ransom: 20 bitcoin demanded, approximately GBP 596,000 at the time. NOT PAID - the library refused, and Rhysida published the data.
nodes.downtime: Services were severely disrupted for months. The main catalogue returned online on 15 January 2024 in read-only format, roughly two and a half months after the attack, with other services expected to remain unavailable for months beyond that. Recovery was complicated by legacy infrastructure and constrained funding, documented in the library's own transparency reporting and subsequent academic analysis.
nodes.data_impact: Approximately 600GB of material leaked publicly after refusal to pay, including internal documents and staff and user data. Full affected-individual counts were not publicly itemised in the reporting reviewed.
nodes.summary: The UK's national library, described as one of the worst cyber incidents in British history. Rhysida rendered almost all VMware ESXi servers unavailable, taking down the website, on-site services and Wi-Fi; the library remained physically open but could accept only cash payments. The institution refused to pay and Rhysida published the stolen material. The case is the reference point for catastrophic recovery severity in a public, non-commercial education/research body: the recovery cost dwarfed the ransom demand by an order of magnitude, and the library had to consume roughly 40% of its financial reserves - a funding mechanism with no analogue in the commercial sector and a key consideration for public-institution insureds.

nodes.id: Educational Services::University of Manchester
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.date: 2023-06-05 (intrusion began 5 June 2023; detected 9 June; containment from 14 June)
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed. No public confirmation of payment; the university worked with the ICO, NCSC and National Crime Agency.
nodes.downtime: Detected 9 June 2023 with containment beginning 14 June. Specific outage duration and full recovery timeline were not publicly disclosed; response ran in parallel with ICO and NCSC engagement.
nodes.data_impact: Around 250GB of data accessed. Included NHS records relating to 1.1 million patients across more than 200 hospitals, gathered for medical research - with NHS numbers and the first three letters of patients' postcodes among the fields, plus major-trauma and terrorist-attack victim treatment data. Separately, student and alumni data was leaked including names, contact details, gender, dates of birth
nodes.summary: The clearest illustration of research-data liability in higher education. Attackers reached a research archive holding NHS patient records gathered from more than 200 hospitals for medical research purposes - including major-trauma patient reports and treatment records for victims of terrorist attacks - alongside current student and alumni data. Attackers then emailed students and staff directly threatening to sell their data, a triple-extortion pressure tactic. The incident triggered questions in UK health and education policy about universities holding national-scale clinical datasets under research governance rather than clinical security controls.

nodes.id: Educational Services::Minneapolis Public Schools (Special School District No. 1)
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.victim: Minneapolis Public Schools (Special School District No. 1)
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed. Costs included forensic investigation, restoration from backups, and notification plus credit monitoring for 105,617 individuals.
nodes.ransom: $1,000,000 demanded by Medusa with a 17 March 2023 deadline; the leak site also offered a $50,000-per-day deadline extension and listed the data for outright purchase at $1 million. NOT PAID - the district restored from internal backups and Medusa published the stolen files.
nodes.downtime: Widespread digital disruption following the 17 February 2023 encryption event; the district recovered encrypted data from internal backups rather than paying. Precise system-restoration duration was not publicly disclosed. Notification took seven months, completing in September 2023.
nodes.data_impact: 105,617 people notified as affected. Nearly 200,000 individual files containing sensitive student and educator information were released publicly, including student psychological and welfare records. Cybersecurity experts confirmed campus security maps and school security blueprints were among the leaked material - creating ongoing physical-safety risk to students.
nodes.summary: The reference case for extortion harm to minors and for notification failure. Medusa demanded $1 million with a 17 March deadline, posted the district on its leak site with a countdown, offered to sell the data to any buyer for $1 million, and offered the district the option to pay $50,000 per additional day of delay. The district refused and restored from internal backups - but Medusa then published the files. Analysts confirmed the leaked corpus included school security blueprints, a physical-safety exposure that cannot be remediated by notification or credit monitoring. The district publicly characterised the event as an 'encryption event' and did not notify the 105,617 affected individuals until September 2023, seven months later.

nodes.id: Educational Services::Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD)
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.date: 2022-09-03 (attack 3 September 2022; leak-site posting 30 September 2022; data published 2 October 2022)
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as a single figure. The district funded incident response, credit monitoring for affected individuals including contractors whose SSNs were exposed, and a subsequent security programme uplift.
nodes.ransom: Demand amount not publicly disclosed. NOT PAID - LAUSD publicly refused, stating public dollars are better spent on students than on criminals, and Vice Society published the data on its leak blog on 2 October 2022.
nodes.downtime: The attack disrupted district systems in early September 2022 at the start of the school year, though schools remained open. Threat actors had persistent access from 31 July to 3 September 2022 before detection - a dwell time of over a month. Full remediation timeline was not publicly disclosed.
nodes.data_impact: 500GB of data stolen and published. The trove included student psychological assessments, health information including COVID-19 test data, and prior conviction reports. LAUSD separately confirmed that contractors' Social Security numbers were among the stolen data. Passport data and other sensitive identifiers were also reported as potentially included.
nodes.summary: The attack that made K-12 ransomware a national policy issue in the US. Vice Society - the group that dominated education targeting in this period, ranking fourth all-time in the Education dataset with 63 victims - dwelled in the network of the second-largest US school district for over a month, from 31 July to 3 September 2022. LAUSD publicly refused to pay on the principle that 'dollars must be used to fund students and education' and that paying never guarantees full recovery, following FBI guidance. Vice Society published the full 500GB trove in retaliation. The leaked data's contents - student psychological assessments, health and COVID-19 test data, and prior conviction reports - established the template for how education extortion inflicts harm on minors specifically.

nodes.id: Energy and Utilities::Colonial Pipeline
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: No single official total disclosed by the company; national gasoline price spiked to a 6+ year high (~$3.04/gal). Ransom of $4.4M paid (see below). Widespread regional economic disruption from fuel shortages.
nodes.ransom: $4.4M paid (75 bitcoin) within hours, overseen by the FBI. On June 7, 2021 the DOJ announced seizure/recovery of 63.7 BTC, then worth ~$2.3M (lower than paid amount due to BTC price drop).
nodes.downtime: All pipeline operations halted May 7; systems and operations returned to normal by May 15 (~6-day shutdown). Decryptor tool from DarkSide was slow, so recovery largely relied on Colonial's own restoration.
nodes.data_impact: Attackers exfiltrated roughly 100GB of data prior to encryption (double-extortion); primary impact was operational/physical rather than a large PII breach.
nodes.summary: The largest refined-fuels pipeline in the US (Houston to the Southeast) was hit by DarkSide ransomware on its IT systems. Colonial proactively halted ALL pipeline operations to contain the attack. The 6-day shutdown interrupted fuel distribution to 17 states, triggering panic-buying, fuel shortages, and the highest average US gasoline price in over six years (~$3.04/gal by May 18). It is the defining cyber-physical energy ransomware case and prompted new TSA pipeline security directives.

nodes.id: Energy and Utilities::Halliburton
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: ~$35M direct pretax cost reported in Q3 2024 results (filed late Oct 2024); ~$0.02 adjusted-EPS impact for the quarter from lost/delayed revenue during system unavailability.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed — Halliburton did not confirm whether a ransom was demanded, negotiated, or paid.
nodes.downtime: Precautionary shutdown of parts of IT infrastructure caused client-system disconnections and temporary inability to generate critical business documents; company described operational impact as limited and restored systems over subsequent weeks. Exact downtime not itemized.
nodes.data_impact: Data exfiltration confirmed; company stated information was taken from its systems. Specific record counts/data types not fully disclosed publicly.
nodes.summary: One of the world's largest oilfield-services companies detected unauthorized access to corporate IT on Aug 21, 2024 and precautionarily shut down certain applications, including production-planning and shipment-tracking systems used in customer delivery. RansomHub claimed the attack and listed the company on its leak site; Halliburton confirmed data was stolen. Disclosed via SEC Form 8-K (Aug 23) and 8-K/A.

nodes.id: Energy and Utilities::Suncor Energy / Petro-Canada
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly quantified as a single figure; disruption spanned 1,500+ retail sites over a weekend plus remediation costs (Suncor replaced employee laptops/computers as part of response).
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed; Suncor characterized it as a 'cybersecurity incident' and did not confirm a ransom.
nodes.downtime: Payment-system disruptions began ~June 21 and were largely resolved over the following days; Suncor swapped out employee computers as a remediation measure, extending internal recovery activity.
nodes.data_impact: Unauthorized party accessed basic information of Petro-Points loyalty members; affected members and privacy regulators were notified. No large-scale financial-data theft publicly confirmed.
nodes.summary: A cybersecurity incident at Canadian integrated-energy giant Suncor disrupted its Petro-Canada retail subsidiary (1,500+ stations). Many stations went cash-only, unable to accept credit/debit or rewards; the Petro-Canada app, Petro-Points login, and car washes were unavailable at various sites. Illustrates downstream retail/payment-system exposure in vertically integrated energy firms.

nodes.id: Energy and Utilities::Encevo Group (Creos & Enovos, Luxembourg)
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed as a dollar figure; operational impact limited to customer-portal outages (no supply interruption).
nodes.ransom: Ransom amount not publicly disclosed; ALPHV threatened to publish stolen data if unpaid.
nodes.downtime: Creos and Enovos customer portals were rendered non-operational following the July 22-23 intrusion; portals were restored over subsequent days/weeks while supply services remained running.
nodes.data_impact: ALPHV claimed exfiltration of 150GB+ across 180,000+ files, published on its leak site July 29 — contracts, agreements, ID copies, invoices, and emails; analyses found 2,270+ files containing plaintext credentials/passwords and 100,000+ documents marked confidential.
nodes.summary: Luxembourg's main energy supplier/distribution group — network operator Creos and supplier Enovos, under parent Encevo — was hit overnight July 22-23, 2022 by ALPHV/BlackCat (the DarkSide/Colonial lineage rebrand). Customer portals of Creos and Enovos were knocked offline, though electricity and gas supply and breakdown services continued uninterrupted. Demonstrates data-exfil-led extortion against European grid infrastructure.

nodes.id: Energy and Utilities::Conpet
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly quantified; company emphasized transport operations were unaffected, limiting operational/financial disruption.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.downtime: Business IT systems were isolated in response; SCADA/telecom and pipeline transport operations remained operational throughout (no OT downtime reported). IT recovery/remediation ongoing after Feb 2026 disclosure.
nodes.data_impact: Qilin alleged exfiltration of ~1TB including financial records, personnel data, and passport scans, and published sample images; Conpet confirmed data was stolen.
nodes.summary: Romania's national oil-pipeline transport operator detected a cyberattack on Feb 3, 2026 affecting its business IT infrastructure. Crucially, OT systems — SCADA and telecommunications — stayed fully functional and pipeline transport continued. Qilin claimed the attack and alleged theft of ~1TB of data. Root cause was an infostealer on an IT administrator's personal device; with valid WSUS credentials attackers abused Conpet's own update infrastructure to push a malicious 'fake update' delivering Qilin ransomware.

nodes.id: Energy and Utilities::Ecopetrol
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed at time of research.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed at time of research.
nodes.downtime: Not publicly disclosed at time of research.
nodes.data_impact: Claimed on ransomware.live leak-tracking; specifics of stolen data not independently confirmed at time of research.
nodes.summary: Ecopetrol, Colombia's state-controlled national oil company and one of Latin America's largest energy firms, was listed as a victim by the 'TheGentlemen' ransomware group on ransomware.live (attack date 2026-07-17). Included as a recent, geographically diverse, large-state-oil-company data point from the ransomware.live Energy sector feed. Detailed public reporting was not yet available at research time (July 19, 2026).

nodes.id: Energy and Utilities::Newpark Resources, Inc.
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: not publicly disclosed
nodes.ransom: not publicly disclosed
nodes.downtime: The incident caused disruptions and limitation of access to certain information systems, but manufacturing and field operations continued utilizing established downtime procedures.
nodes.data_impact: not publicly disclosed
nodes.summary: On October 29, 2024, Newpark Resources, Inc. detected a ransomware incident where an unauthorized third party accessed its internal information systems. The company activated its cybersecurity response plan and is investigating the incident with external advisors.

nodes.id: Finance and Insurance::CNA Financial Corporation
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Reportedly paid $40 million in ransom - among the largest ransom payments publicly reported at the time. Full cost of remediation/legal/breach-notification beyond the ransom itself is not publicly disclosed in aggregate.
nodes.ransom: Attackers initially demanded $60 million; CNA paid approximately $40 million roughly two weeks after data theft began.
nodes.downtime: Multi-week disruption to remote access, corporate email, and phone systems; CNA stated it was able to recover encrypted/stolen data with no indication the exfiltrated data was viewed, retained, or shared further after payment.
nodes.data_impact: Corporate and some employee/customer data was copied/exfiltrated prior to encryption; CNA said no indication the data was subsequently misused, though the scope of records affected was not fully broken out publicly.
nodes.summary: One of the largest U.S. commercial insurers was hit by a new variant of Phoenix CryptoLocker (attributed to the Russia-linked Evil Corp syndicate). Attackers accessed systems from March 5-21, 2021, exfiltrating data before deploying ransomware and knocking core systems offline, including remote access, email, and phone systems.

nodes.id: Finance and Insurance::Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) - U.S. broker-dealer/financial services unit
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.victim: Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) - U.S. broker-dealer/financial services unit
nodes.financial_impact: Not a disclosed single dollar loss figure for ICBC itself, but market-wide impact was measurable: more than $62 billion of U.S. Treasurys reportedly failed to deliver on one day, and settlement of over $9 billion in Treasury-backed assets was disrupted.
nodes.ransom: No ransom amount publicly confirmed as demanded or paid by ICBC.
nodes.downtime: ICBC's unit lost access to corporate email and had to physically courier settlement details via USB stick to counterparties in Manhattan while systems were restored; disruption lasted several days before normal electronic settlement resumed.
nodes.data_impact: Data exfiltration/theft was claimed by LockBit but the specific volume/type of records taken was not comprehensively disclosed publicly.
nodes.summary: LockBit compromised ICBC's U.S. financial-services division (believed via Citrix NetScaler vulnerabilities CVE-2023-4966/4967), disrupting settlement of U.S. Treasury trades and repo financing at the world's largest bank by assets - a rare ransomware incident with visible, market-wide operational impact.

nodes.id: Finance and Insurance::Fidelity National Financial (FNF)
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Specific dollar cost of the incident (remediation, business interruption, legal) not publicly broken out by FNF; real estate closings nationwide were delayed for the outage period, an indirect economic impact not quantified publicly.
nodes.ransom: No official ransom figure disclosed by FNF; ALPHV's swift removal of FNF from its leak site is widely read by researchers as an indicator a payment was made, but this is inference, not confirmed disclosure.
nodes.downtime: Systems were offline for nearly a week, disrupting title/escrow closings for home buyers and real estate agents nationwide during that period.
nodes.data_impact: Data of approximately 1.3 million individuals was confirmed stolen and subject to breach notification.
nodes.summary: A Fortune 500 title-insurance and real-estate services provider (handles closings for a large share of U.S. home sales) had systems taken offline for about a week; ALPHV/BlackCat claimed the intrusion, and the gang's removal of FNF from its leak site is widely interpreted as a sign a ransom was paid.

nodes.id: Finance and Insurance::ION Group / ION Cleared Derivatives
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.country: United Kingdom (global client base incl. U.S., Europe)
nodes.financial_impact: No public disclosure of direct financial loss to ION or its clients; the incident's significance was systemic/operational (derivatives clearing workflow disruption) rather than a disclosed dollar figure.
nodes.ransom: LockBit threatened to publish stolen data by February 4, 2023 if unpaid; no ransom amount or payment/non-payment was publicly confirmed by ION.
nodes.downtime: Affected servers were isolated and the incident contained to a specific environment; several days of manual/workaround trade processing for affected clients while remediation continued.
nodes.data_impact: LockBit claimed data was exfiltrated during the intrusion; scope/type of data was not comprehensively disclosed publicly by ION.
nodes.summary: A UK-based financial software vendor whose platforms underpin derivatives clearing/trading for major banks and brokers was hit by LockBit, forcing at least 42 clients - including major U.S. and European financial institutions - to fall back to manual trade processing for cleared derivatives.

nodes.id: Finance and Insurance::Evolve Bank & Trust
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Specific dollar cost not publicly disclosed by Evolve; the company offered two years of free credit monitoring/identity protection to affected individuals, an ongoing cost not quantified publicly. Reputational/partner-relationship impact on its fintech clients was significant but not dollar-quantified.
nodes.ransom: Evolve confirmed it did NOT pay the ransom demand (amount not publicly disclosed), leading LockBit to publish the stolen data.
nodes.downtime: Attackers accessed and downloaded data from Evolve's databases/file shares over a window from February to May 2024 before the bank discovered the intrusion in May 2024; public notification did not begin until July 8, 2024.
nodes.data_impact: At least 7.6 million individuals' personal data affected, including names, Social Security numbers, bank account details, card PANs, wire/settlement files, in clear text; downstream fintech partners (Affirm, Mercury, Wise, and others) were also impacted.
nodes.summary: A U.S. banking-as-a-service (BaaS) bank whose infrastructure underpins numerous fintech apps (e.g., Affirm, Wise, Mercury) was breached after an employee clicked a malicious link; Evolve refused to pay, so LockBit published the stolen data, exposing both direct banking customers and downstream fintech partner customers - a clear third-party/supply-chain risk case for the sector.

nodes.id: Finance and Insurance::Central Bank of Libya
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.date: Disclosed June 9, 2026; Qilin claimed responsibility June 22, 2026
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed. The bank characterized the incident as affecting only a limited set of systems, with no reported disruption to national payment operations.
nodes.ransom: No ransom amount publicly disclosed or confirmed.
nodes.downtime: Bank stated the incident was 'fully contained' as of late June 2026, with recovery/system restoration ongoing per an internal plan; no extended public-facing outage reported.
nodes.data_impact: Qilin threatened to release confidential banking data but as of the incident's public reporting, the specific volume/type of data was not independently confirmed or publicly itemized.
nodes.summary: Libya's central bank disclosed a cyberattack affecting a limited number of systems/technical services; the Qilin ransomware-as-a-service operation later publicly claimed the breach and threatened to release confidential banking data, illustrating ransomware's expansion into national financial-infrastructure/central-bank targets.

nodes.id: Finance and Insurance::Frost Bank and Citizens Financial Group (Citizens Bank) - shared third-party vendor breach
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.victim: Frost Bank and Citizens Financial Group (Citizens Bank) - shared third-party vendor breach
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed by either bank in dollar terms; both institutions face customer class-action lawsuits alleging inadequate safeguarding of data via the vendor relationship, with litigation costs not yet quantified publicly.
nodes.ransom: No ransom amount publicly disclosed; Everest gave a six-day deadline before threatening to publish the full data dump.
nodes.downtime: Both banks stated their own core systems were not directly breached (the incident occurred in the third-party vendor's environment); no extended outage of banking services was reported.
nodes.data_impact: Everest claimed roughly 250,000 Frost Bank client records (Social Security numbers, tax IDs, names, mortgage rates, investment/income data, home addresses) and additional Citizens Bank records, with combined exposure reported by researchers at up to approximately 3.65 million records across both institutions.
nodes.summary: The Everest ransomware gang claimed breaches of two unrelated major U.S. banks, Frost Bank (San Antonio) and Citizens Financial Group, tracing back to a single shared third-party vendor that handled statement printing (for Citizens) and tax-document fulfillment (for Frost) - a textbook example of concentrated third-party/vendor risk in the financial sector, since one vendor compromise exposed customers of multiple unrelated institutions.

nodes.id: Finance and Insurance::Deutsche Bank (via third-party marketing/incentive platform vendor)
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.victim: Deutsche Bank (via third-party marketing/incentive platform vendor)
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.downtime: No disruption to core Deutsche Bank banking services reported; investigation of the third-party provider's environment was ongoing at time of disclosure.
nodes.data_impact: Group claimed employee email addresses, password hashes, and physical mailing addresses among the exposed records; scope limited to data held within the third-party marketing/incentive platform rather than core customer banking data, per Deutsche Bank's statement.
nodes.summary: The 'Unsafe' ransomware-as-a-service group added Deutsche Bank to its leak site, posting screenshots purporting to show database exports (employee emails, password hashes, mailing addresses). Deutsche Bank clarified the actual incident occurred at an external German service provider operating a marketing/incentive platform for the bank's sales partners, not within Deutsche Bank's own core banking environment - another illustration of third-party/vendor exposure at a major global bank.

nodes.id: Finance and Insurance::Prudential Financial, Inc.

nodes.id: Finance and Insurance::Globe Life Inc.

The company activated its incident response plan and is cooperating with federal law enforcement while investigating the claims made by the threat actor.

nodes.id: Healthcare and Social Assistance::Change Healthcare (subsidiary of UnitedHealth Group/Optum)
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.date: Attack began February 21, 2024; disclosed February 2024; extortion/data-listing activity continued into April 2024
nodes.financial_impact: UnitedHealth Group's total reported cyberattack impact reached approximately $2.9 billion for fiscal year 2024 (direct response costs plus business disruption); an initial Q1 2024 estimate of $0.74/share grew through the year to a full-year estimate of $1.90-$2.05/share. UnitedHealth also advanced more than $9 billion in interim/interest-free funding to affected providers by Q2 2024 to offset cash-flow disruption across the industry.
nodes.ransom: UnitedHealth confirmed paying a ransom reported by multiple outlets at roughly $22 million in bitcoin to the ALPHV/BlackCat affiliate; a second group (RansomHub) subsequently claimed to still hold the stolen data and re-extorted the company.
nodes.downtime: Core clearinghouse and pharmacy/claims systems were down for multiple weeks beginning February 21, 2024, with a phased, multi-month restoration of full transaction volumes through spring 2024.
nodes.data_impact: UnitedHealth later disclosed the breach affected the personal/health information of approximately 190 million individuals (one of the largest healthcare data breaches ever reported to HHS), including medical records, billing/claims data, SSNs, and insurance information.
nodes.summary: The largest and most disruptive healthcare ransomware incident on record. Attackers used compromised credentials to access a Citrix portal lacking multi-factor authentication, then deployed ransomware against Change Healthcare, the dominant US claims clearinghouse processing roughly one-third of all patient records and ~15 billion transactions annually. The outage froze prescription processing, insurance eligibility checks, and provider payments nationwide for weeks.

nodes.id: Healthcare and Social Assistance::Universal Health Services (UHS) — ~400 US hospitals/care sites
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.victim: Universal Health Services (UHS) — ~400 US hospitals/care sites
nodes.financial_impact: UHS reported approximately $67 million in total pre-tax losses tied to the attack (lost operating income, reduced patient activity, billing-delay reserves, and recovery costs), and stated it expected to recover most of this through cyber insurance.
nodes.ransom: UHS did not pay a ransom and recovered from backups; no confirmed ransom amount was publicly reported.
nodes.downtime: EHR and other core IT applications were down across all ~400 UHS care sites for roughly three weeks before full restoration.
nodes.data_impact: No large-scale confirmed public data leak was widely reported for this incident (Ryuk at the time was primarily an encryption-only/non-exfiltration operation); primary impact was operational/clinical disruption rather than a mass PHI leak.
nodes.summary: One of the earliest large-scale hospital-system ransomware attacks; Ryuk encrypted IT systems across UHS's national network, forcing staff onto paper documentation, diverting ambulances, and suspending IT applications company-wide.

nodes.id: Healthcare and Social Assistance::Health Service Executive (HSE) — Ireland's national public health system
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.victim: Health Service Executive (HSE) — Ireland's national public health system
nodes.financial_impact: Estimates for recovery costs varied widely across reporting: the HSE's director general cited a June 2021 estimate exceeding $600 million; other analyses put full recovery cost at roughly $100 million, and yet other reporting cited about $83 million; figures differ by scope (pure IT rebuild vs. total health-system impact) and are not fully reconciled in public reporting.
nodes.ransom: Conti demanded $19,999,000; the HSE refused to pay and instead worked with Ireland's National Cyber Security Centre; a free decryptor was later released by the attackers.
nodes.downtime: National IT systems were shut down immediately upon detection; full recovery across the health system took approximately four months.
nodes.data_impact: Patient data was exfiltrated and reportedly used to attempt individual extortion of patients; Ireland's HSE has since (as of reporting around 2025) offered approximately EUR750 in compensation to affected individuals whose personal data was compromised.
nodes.summary: A nationwide ransomware attack that forced Ireland's entire public health IT infrastructure offline, disrupting hospital appointments, cancer treatment scheduling, radiology, and COVID-19 vaccine registration systems across the country. Conti later provided a free decryptor under international pressure but retained and later leveraged stolen patient data.

nodes.id: Healthcare and Social Assistance::CommonSpirit Health — ~140+ hospitals across ~13 US states
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.victim: CommonSpirit Health — ~140+ hospitals across ~13 US states
nodes.date: Initial access September 16, 2022; ransomware detected/disclosed October 2-3, 2022
nodes.financial_impact: CommonSpirit initially estimated the cost at approximately $150 million, later revising the total to approximately $160 million (business interruption, remediation, and related expenses) as reported in 2023 disclosures.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.downtime: Multi-week system outages beginning October 2022 affecting more than 100-160+ facilities; precise full-recovery date not specified in public reporting.
nodes.data_impact: Personal data of more than 623,700 patients was reported exposed; the breach affected over 150 facilities and led to two class-action lawsuits.
nodes.summary: One of the largest US nonprofit hospital operators was forced to take systems offline across more than 100 facilities in at least 13 states, delaying access to EHRs and disrupting patient care, following network compromise weeks before the ransomware deployment was detected.

nodes.id: Healthcare and Social Assistance::Lehigh Valley Health Network (LVHN)
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: LVHN agreed to a $65 million class-action settlement (finalized November 2024), one of the largest healthcare ransomware-related settlements on record; of this, $52 million was earmarked for patients whose nude treatment images were published.
nodes.ransom: LVHN refused to pay the ransom; the specific dollar amount demanded was not publicly disclosed.
nodes.downtime: Specific system-downtime duration not publicly detailed in available reporting; the affected system was a specific practice's oncology imaging network rather than network-wide LVHN infrastructure.
nodes.data_impact: More than 134,000 patients were affected/eligible for settlement compensation; leaked data included sensitive treatment photographs and other PHI published on BlackCat's leak site.
nodes.summary: Attackers compromised a network supporting a Lackawanna County physician practice, including a radiation-oncology imaging system, and — after LVHN refused to pay — published highly sensitive clinical photos of breast cancer patients (nude from the waist up) to pressure payment, an unusually aggressive harassment-based extortion tactic.

nodes.id: Healthcare and Social Assistance::Medibank Private (major Australian health insurer)
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.date: Attack detected October 2022; extortion/data leaks began November 2022
nodes.financial_impact: Not fully quantified in a single public figure in the sources reviewed; the incident drove significant remediation, regulatory, and reputational costs and a multi-year AFP-led international investigation; precise total company cost not publicly disclosed in the sources found.
nodes.ransom: Initial demand of roughly US$10 million (A$15 million), later reduced to approximately US$9.7 million; Medibank refused to pay, consistent with Australian government guidance against ransom payments.
nodes.downtime: Primarily a data-theft/extortion event rather than an encryption/operational-outage event; core insurance operations were not reported as extensively down.
nodes.data_impact: Personal and health data of approximately 9.7 million current and former customers was compromised, including about 1.8 million international customers; data included Medicare, passport, and driver's licence numbers plus sensitive medical history.
nodes.summary: Attackers stole and threatened to publish highly sensitive personal and health data of Medibank's customers, including records revealing abortions, addiction treatment, and mental-health conditions, after the insurer refused a ransom demand — one of Australia's largest ever data breaches and a landmark case in international ransomware attribution/sanctions.

nodes.id: Healthcare and Social Assistance::Synnovis (pathology/blood-testing partner for NHS trusts in London)
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.victim: Synnovis (pathology/blood-testing partner for NHS trusts in London)
nodes.financial_impact: Specific total financial cost to Synnovis or the NHS trusts was not found publicly quantified in a single disclosed figure in the sources reviewed; disruption was extensive across South-East London NHS services for months.
nodes.ransom: Not publicly disclosed.
nodes.downtime: Severe disruption began June 3, 2024, with over 11,000 outpatient/elective procedure appointments delayed; some services were affected for months, with normal service levels reported restored by December 2024 — roughly six months.
nodes.data_impact: Qilin published approximately 400GB of stolen data on June 20, 2024, including patient names, NHS numbers, and descriptions of blood tests.
nodes.summary: A ransomware attack on a third-party pathology provider partnered with Guy's and St Thomas' and King's College Hospital NHS Trusts caused a critical shortage of O-negative blood, cancelled thousands of appointments and procedures, and was later formally identified as a contributing factor in a patient death — one of the clearest documented cases of ransomware causing loss of life via a healthcare supply-chain/third-party vector.

nodes.summary: On April 6, 2023, Enzo Biochem, Inc. experienced a ransomware attack that impacted its IT systems. The Company implemented containment measures and launched an investigation, discovering that certain data was extracted from its systems as part of the incident.

nodes.id: Information Technology::Kaseya (VSA platform)
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Direct financial loss to Kaseya not publicly disclosed; downstream impact spanned 800-1,500 businesses across ~17 countries (e.g., Sweden's Coop grocery chain closed ~800 stores). Broader economic cost not authoritatively quantified.
nodes.ransom: REvil demanded a single universal-decryptor payment of $70 million in Bitcoin. Kaseya states it did NOT pay the ransom; it obtained a universal decryptor from a 'trusted third party' (later reported as provided via the FBI).
nodes.downtime: VSA SaaS and on-prem servers taken offline as a precaution on July 2; patched VSA restored around July 11-12; a universal decryptor was distributed on July 22-23, 2021 to help victims restore data. Recovery for downstream MSP clients ran days to weeks.
nodes.data_impact: Primarily encryption/availability impact rather than mass data theft; up to ~1,500 downstream organizations had systems encrypted.
nodes.summary: REvil exploited zero-day vulnerabilities in Kaseya's VSA remote-monitoring-and-management software to push ransomware through ~60 direct MSP customers to their downstream clients — the archetypal IT supply-chain cascade attack.

nodes.id: Information Technology::Progress Software (MOVEit Transfer)
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Aggregate downstream cost estimated by Emsisoft at roughly $10.6B-$15.8B (using IBM's per-record cost); some scaled estimates ran far higher. Progress Software's own direct costs not fully disclosed; it faced an SEC investigation and dozens of class-action lawsuits (40M+ claimants).
nodes.ransom: Clop did not encrypt systems; it demanded extortion payments from individual victim organizations (amounts varied and were not publicly itemized). Many victims declined to pay.
nodes.downtime: This was a data-theft (not encryption) event, so impact was breach-remediation and notification rather than operational downtime; remediation and victim-notification stretched over many months into 2024.
nodes.data_impact: Over 2,700 organizations confirmed impacted and approximately 93.3 million individuals' personal data exposed (estimates ranged 64M-95M+ over time).
nodes.summary: Clop mass-exploited a zero-day SQL-injection flaw (CVE-2023-34362) in Progress Software's MOVEit managed-file-transfer product to steal data from thousands of organizations worldwide — one of the largest supply-chain data-extortion campaigns on record.

nodes.id: Information Technology::CDK Global
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Anderson Economic Group estimated total dealer losses exceeding $1 billion (revised up from ~$944M) from roughly two-plus weeks of disruption.
nodes.ransom: BlackSuit initially demanded ~$10M, reportedly escalating toward $50M+. CDK is widely reported to have paid approximately $25 million in Bitcoin (wallets tied to BlackSuit received ~$25M about two days after the attack, per CyberScoop).
nodes.downtime: Dealerships reverted to manual/pen-and-paper processes for nearly two weeks; CDK announced services restored for nearly all dealerships by around July 4, 2024.
nodes.data_impact: Primarily operational outage; extent of any data exfiltration less publicly quantified than the operational and financial disruption.
nodes.summary: BlackSuit ransomware crippled CDK Global's Dealer Management System SaaS, which powers operations for ~15,000 auto dealerships across the U.S. and Canada; a second intrusion during recovery on June 19 prolonged the outage.

nodes.id: Information Technology::Ingram Micro
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Specific revenue loss not publicly disclosed; multi-day global halt of order processing at a distributor with ~$48B annual revenue implies material lost/delayed transactions, though the company did not quantify it publicly.
nodes.ransom: Ransom amount not publicly disclosed; on July 29-30, 2025 SafePay threatened to leak ~3.5TB of allegedly stolen data unless paid. No confirmation of payment.
nodes.downtime: Systems failed around 8:00 AM ET on July 3; website and staged order processing resumed July 7-8; the company reported operations back to normal worldwide by July 9, 2025.
nodes.data_impact: Reported exposure of personal data of over 42,000 employees and applicants; SafePay claimed ~3.5TB of data.
nodes.summary: SafePay ransomware caused a global outage at Ingram Micro, one of the world's largest IT distributors; intrusion is attributed to compromised credentials on the Palo Alto GlobalProtect VPN, halting worldwide order processing.

nodes.id: Information Technology::Quanta Computer (Apple supplier)
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed. Impact was primarily reputational and IP-confidentiality loss (leaked device blueprints) rather than reported revenue loss.
nodes.ransom: REvil demanded $50 million, reportedly escalating toward $100M; the ransom was not paid by Quanta (and REvil eventually removed the leaked files). No confirmed payment.
nodes.downtime: Operational downtime not the primary reported impact; this was chiefly a data-exfiltration/IP-leak extortion event.
nodes.data_impact: Theft and partial publication of confidential design schematics/blueprints for unreleased Apple devices (MacBook, Apple Watch drawings).
nodes.summary: After Quanta (a major Apple ODM) declined to pay, REvil pivoted to extort Apple directly, publishing stolen schematics for unreleased products, timed to Apple's 'Spring Loaded' launch event — a landmark IP-theft extortion in the tech hardware supply chain.

nodes.id: Information Technology::Software AG
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Direct financial loss not fully disclosed; the company reported internal-network disruption but said customer-facing cloud services were unaffected.
nodes.ransom: Clop demanded approximately $23 million. Software AG refused to pay.
nodes.downtime: Internal network, help desk and some internal communications were disrupted for a period in October 2020; customer cloud services remained operational.
nodes.data_impact: About 1TB of data stolen, including employee passport/ID data, health-related documents and internal emails; screenshots and files leaked publicly after negotiations broke down.
nodes.summary: Clop ransomware struck German enterprise-software giant Software AG, encrypting internal systems and stealing about 1TB of data, then publishing files after the company refused to negotiate — an early high-profile double-extortion case in the software industry.

nodes.id: Information Technology::Tata Technologies
nodes.label: Incident
nodes.financial_impact: Not publicly disclosed; the company said client-delivery services remained unaffected. No quantified revenue loss reported.
nodes.ransom: Specific ransom amount not disclosed; Hunters International threatened public release of the data and, when unpaid, leaked it (~730,000 files) on its dark-web site in March 2025.
nodes.downtime: Temporary disruption to some IT services per the January stock-exchange disclosure; client delivery reported unaffected. Detailed recovery timeline not publicly quantified.
nodes.data_impact: Claimed theft of 1.4TB (~730,000 files) including current/former employee personal details, purchase orders and confidential customer contracts (India and U.S. customers).
nodes.summary: Hunters International claimed a January 2025 ransomware attack on Tata Technologies (engineering/IT-services arm of the Tata group), later leaking 1.4TB of stolen data; Tata Motors disclosed a ransomware incident to Indian stock exchanges.
